UNEASY APPLY

Lawmakers take aim at job listings that ghosted you

Illustration: Morning Brew Inc., Photo: Unsplash

The government can’t do anything about your Hinge matches—unless they run a company that’s posting about roles that may not actually be open, aka ‘ghost jobs.’ These types of listings, which attract applicants but lead to no hiring activity, are running so rampant that lawmakers across the country are working to get ’em banned, the Wall Street Journal reported yesterday.

Your résumé isn’t chopped, you may just be applying to jobs that employers have either already filled or never intended to fill. You can sometimes recognize them as the listings that sound too good to be true and stay posted for months:

  • Roughly one in five listings advertised on online job boards per quarter are ghost jobs, according to the hiring platform Greenhouse.
  • This phenomenon is reportedly getting worse, but it’s been wrecking egos for a while. About 81% of recruiters said in a 2024 MyPerfectResume survey that their employers posted ghost job ads.

Here’s what lawmakers are doing about it

New York state legislators recently passed a bill (now awaiting the governor’s signature) that would fine employers if they don’t mention expected hiring timelines in their job postings. Lawmakers in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, and California are considering similar reforms.

Meanwhile, Texas is going after the middleman. The state’s Attorney General Ken Paxton opened an investigation into LinkedIn last month, alleging that the platform promotes and profits from ghost jobs.

Why do employers even post ghost jobs?

In the corporate version of “hey sorry I’ve been so busy recently,” an employer might’ve approved an opening, nixed it, and then been slow to remove the job post.

But that’s a best-case explanation. According to the 2024 MyPerfectResume survey, 38% of recruiters post fake jobs to stay relevant on job boards when they’re not hiring, while 36% do it to test their listing’s effectiveness. Meanwhile, some job seekers think employers promote ghost jobs to harvest applicants’ data or to convince investors that the company is growing.—ML

World

Tour de headlines

Geoff Robins/Getty Images

🇺🇸🇨🇦 US and Canada fail to reach a deal to stave off 50% tariffs. As of last night the Trump administration is imposing a 50% import tax on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, after talks to reach a trade deal before the 12:01am deadline for the tariffs to kick in collapsed at the last minute. Earlier in the week, a draft agreement seen by news outlets would have had the US lowering tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, and autos in exchange for Canada scrapping the retaliatory measures it has taken since Trump began his trade war—but negotiators couldn’t get it across the finish line. Each country blamed the other for the failure to finalize an agreement, and Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada would retaliate “dollar for dollar” for the new tariffs.

🥩 Trump to allow tariff-free beef imports to bring prices down. President Trump wants the burgers at your Labor Day cookout to be cheaper: He said on Truth Social that the US will “allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out of quota tariff” over the next three months. He said the beef would be sold at 25% below current market prices. The move comes after recent data showed that beef sales volumes for a 13-week period that included big burger days Memorial Day and July Fourth dipped 0.3% compared to last year, suggesting that high prices could be putting consumers off beef. However, a US beef industry association criticized the decision to allow cheap imports, saying it wouldn’t address the root problem of high prices: America needing to increase the size of its beef herd.

🏗️ SCOTUS allows White House ballroom construction for now. A lower court’s order that would have halted construction of the $400 million ballroom President Trump is adding to the White House (based on a ruling that it requires Congressional approval) would have taken effect yesterday, but the Supreme Court stepped in because of the president’s emergency appeal. Yesterday’s decision, a one-sentence order from Chief Justice John Roberts, isn’t a final ruling in the case. But it does permit construction of the ballroom, which was already proceeding following the demolition of the East Wing, to continue as the Supreme Court considers the matter.—AR

GOOD FOR THE SEOUL

How Seoul became the busiest international airport

Olga Pak / Getty Images

As a result of turmoil in the Middle East, Dubai’s 12-year reign as the top destination for international travelers is over. Seoul’s Incheon Airport has become the world’s busiest hub for international travel over the first six months of this year, according to data from Airports Council International (ACI).

Since the Iran war started in February, the shift away from the city where Tom Cruise climbed the Burj Khalifa has been drastic:

  • The number of international passengers going through Dubai fell from 7.4 million in February to 2.5 million in March (but rose to 4.7 million in June).
  • Meanwhile, Incheon in Seoul served 38.4 million international travelers in the first half of the year.

Lost connection: Transfer traffic in the Middle East has fallen by half since the war began, according to the New York Times. Much of that traffic is going through Asia instead: From January to June, Incheon saw an 18% rise in flyers making a connecting flight and a 63% increase in passengers connecting to Europe, compared to a year earlier.

Plan ahead: The International Air Transport Association reported that bookings are down in the Middle East for June through September. But they’re up 33% from a year ago in the Asia-Pacific region for the same time period.—DL

➡️ A 15-foot python named after Jodie Foster (really) became the first snake to receive electrochemotherapy—a breakthrough cancer treatment used in humans—to treat a malignant tumor in her jaw. Crowd work

Last week, we asked, “What’s your favorite building near where you live?” Here are some of our favorite responses:

  • “The Imperial Hotel building in downtown Longmont, CO. It’s a beautiful, three-story, Italianate-style building that’s been converted into apartments and dining. It has the oldest still-open café in the city on the ground floor and live music downstairs, a gorgeous foyer and main staircase (currently under remodel), and is generally the epitome of city history meets local art. I’m lucky enough to work inside.”—Ria from Colorado
  • “The ‘pink building,’ aka Edgewater Beach Apartments, in Chicago. It opened in 1928 as apartments as part of the Edgewater Beach Hotel complex. The hotel was razed in the ’70s, but the apartments, now a co-op, remain.”—Mary from Chicago
  • “The ‘world’s littlest skyscraper’ is a four-story, 40-foot-tall structure located in downtown Wichita Falls, Texas. Built in 1919 during a local oil boom, it resulted from a legendary con where the promoter used blueprints drafted in inches instead of feet to pocket $200,000.”—Terry from Wichita Falls, TX
  • “The 320 South Boston Building in Tulsa, OK! After opening in 1917, it served as the main bank for the ‘Oil Capital of the World.’ It features a 55-ton vault door, underground tunnels connected to neighboring buildings, the first (and still operating) escalator in Tulsa, a ‘weather teller’ light system on its roof to alert citizens of incoming weather, and a rumored mooring station on its cupola for blimps!”—Jackson from Tulsa, OK
  • “House on the Rock, in Spring Green, WI. Easily the most bizarre collection of whimsy, both real and fake! Hours of endless entertainment!”—Sara from Wisconsin
  • “The Garden City UFO House. It’s a hurricane-resistant concrete home that looks like a flying saucer. Located on a narrow sandy peninsula in Garden City Beach, SC, with the Atlantic Ocean on one side and Murrells Inlet on the other. You get an otherworldly sensation of it hovering above the mist when viewing it on foggy mornings.”—Mike from Socastee, SC
